881.event_title: Aurangzeb confines his father Shah Jahan in Agra Fort
881.event: After the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan fell ill in 1657, his sons fought a war of succession, and his son Aurangzeb emerged victorious and took the throne in 1658. Aurangzeb had his father confined in Agra Fort, where Shah Jahan remained for about eight years until his death in January 1666. He was buried in the Taj Mahal beside his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
881.explanation: The emperor who had built the most famous monument of devotion to family spent his last years a prisoner of his own son.
881.tie_back: The kural says the closeness of one's own people, like shade and water, becomes painful when it turns harmful, as Shah Jahan found when his son became his jailer.
881._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of kin turning from comfort into harm, though the kural's shade-and-water simile is about a gradual souring rather than a seizure of power.

882.event_title: Kim Philby is exposed as a Soviet agent inside British intelligence
882.event: Kim Philby became a Soviet agent while at Cambridge in the 1930s, joined Britain's Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) in 1940, rose to head its counter-espionage section, and in 1949 became its chief liaison officer in Washington, passing detailed information about British and American intelligence to Moscow. Suspected after two fellow agents fled in 1951, he was eventually confronted in Beirut in January 1963 by his old friend and MI6 colleague Nicholas Elliott and gave a partial confession. Within days he fled to the Soviet Union, where he lived until his death in 1988.
882.explanation: The most damaging enemy of British intelligence was not a foreign agent kept at arm's length but a trusted colleague and friend at its heart.
882.tie_back: The kural says to fear not the open enemy like a drawn sword but the one who poses as one's own, and Philby did his harm precisely through the trust of his colleagues.
882._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the foe who seems a friend, with the harm flowing from long, trusted association.

883.event_title: Kobayakawa Hideaki changes sides at Sekigahara
883.event: At the Battle of Sekigahara the western coalition led by Ishida Mitsunari faced the eastern army of Tokugawa Ieyasu. Kobayakawa Hideaki, whose troops were posted on Mount Matsuo as part of the western army, had secretly promised to support Ieyasu; during the battle he led his forces down the mountain against his nominal ally Otani Yoshitsugu, and other commanders switched sides with him. The collapse that followed destroyed the western army and opened the way for Tokugawa rule.
883.explanation: The western coalition was undone not by the enemy facing it but by a commander standing within its own lines.
883.tie_back: The kural warns that the enemy within strikes at the moment of weakness and cuts as surely as the potter's tool, as Kobayakawa's turn did at the battle's turning point.
883._accuracy_note: A very close fit for the hidden enemy who strikes at the critical moment; some historians now debate how early Kobayakawa committed to the east, so details of his hesitation are left out.

884.event_title: The sons of Louis the Pious rise against their father
884.place: Frankish Empire (near Colmar and at Compiegne and Soissons, present-day France)
884.event: Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, faced a revolt by his older sons in 830 after he sought to provide a kingdom for Charles, his son by a second marriage. In 833 his sons Lothar, Pippin and Louis met him near Colmar at the place later called the Field of Lies, where his own followers deserted him; he was deposed and made to perform public penance. He was restored in 834 when the younger sons turned against Lothar, but the quarrels continued, and after his death the empire was divided among his sons by the Treaty of Verdun in 843.
884.explanation: The family quarrel at the top of the Carolingian empire turned father against sons and brother against brother, and ended in the division of Charlemagne's realm.
884.tie_back: The kural says hidden enmity in an unreconciled mind brings troubles that turn one's own people against one, as it did within Louis the Pious's family.
884._accuracy_note: A good illustration of inner discord turning kin into opponents, though whose unreformed mind was at fault is a matter of interpretation.

885.event_title: Kublai Khan and his brother Ariq Boke fight for the Mongol throne
885.event: After the death of the Great Khan Mongke in 1259, his brothers Kublai and Ariq Boke each had himself proclaimed Great Khan in 1260, Kublai at Shangdu and Ariq Boke at Karakorum. The brothers fought a four-year civil war that ended when Ariq Boke submitted in 1264; he died in captivity two years later. The struggle left the Mongol empire effectively split into separate khanates, and Kublai concentrated on China, where he founded the Yuan dynasty.
885.explanation: A war between brothers broke the unity of the largest land empire in history, which never again acted as one.
885.tie_back: The kural says enmity that springs from kinship brings deadly evils, and the brothers' war cost the Mongol empire its unity.
885._accuracy_note: A strong fit for deadly enmity within a ruling family, close to the dynastic reading of the traditional commentary.

886.event_title: Athens and Sparta fight the Peloponnesian War
886.event: Athens and Sparta had fought together against the Persian invasions, but rivalry over Athenian power in the Delian League led to the Peloponnesian War, fought from 431 to 404 BCE and ending in Athens' defeat. The Greek city-states continued fighting among themselves for decades afterwards. Weakened by this infighting, they were defeated by Philip II of Macedon at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, after which they lost their independence.
886.explanation: The cities that had united to save Greece from Persia wore each other down until an outside power could master them all.
886.tie_back: The kural says that once discord takes hold among those who were united, it is ever hard to escape destruction, as the Greek city-states found.
886._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of former allies falling out and losing their independence, although the path from the war to Chaeronea spanned more than sixty years.

887.event_title: The United Arab Republic of Egypt and Syria breaks apart
887.event: On 1 February 1958 Egypt and Syria proclaimed their union as the United Arab Republic under Gamal Abdel Nasser, and the union was approved by plebiscites later that month. Egyptian dominance of the union antagonized many Syrians, and on 28 September 1961, after a military coup in Damascus, Syria declared itself independent again. Egypt kept the name United Arab Republic until 1971.
887.explanation: A union that looked complete on paper never became one in spirit and came apart within three and a half years.
887.tie_back: The kural says a group divided by hidden enmity may look joined like a casket and its lid yet never truly unite, which describes the brief union of Egypt and Syria.
887._accuracy_note: A good fit for an outward union lacking inner unity, though the kural speaks of a family or community rather than two states.

888.event: After Emperor Andronicus III died in 1341, John Cantacuzenus, who claimed the regency, and the court of the young John V, led by the empress Anna of Savoy, fell into civil war, and Cantacuzenus proclaimed himself emperor. During the war he allied with the Ottoman Turks and in 1347 retook Constantinople with Turkish help, becoming co-emperor. The fighting ruined much of what remained of the Byzantine economy, allowed the Serbian ruler Stefan Dushan to seize large territories, and helped the Ottomans gain their first foothold in Europe at Gallipoli in 1354.
888.explanation: Six years of fighting between rival factions within the court wore away the strength of an empire already in decline and invited in the power that would later conquer it.
888.tie_back: The kural pictures a house afflicted by internal enmity wearing itself away like metal under a file, which is what the civil war did to Byzantium.
888._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of strength worn away by internal strife, with the empire's own factions doing the damage.

889.event_title: A single deputy's objection breaks up the Polish Sejm
889.event: In 1652 a single deputy, Wladyslaw Sicinski, objected to extending the session of the Sejm, and his lone protest ended it, the first time the principle known as the liberum veto was used to break up a parliament. Under the practice, any one member could defeat a measure or dissolve a session and nullify its acts, and it was later used so often that business was frequently paralysed and foreign powers bribed deputies to use it. The veto was abolished only in the Constitution of 3 May 1791, shortly before the Commonwealth was partitioned out of existence in 1795.
889.explanation: A rule that let the smallest dissent paralyse the whole state became one of the main weaknesses of the Commonwealth.
889.tie_back: The kural says that even internal enmity as small as a split sesame seed holds ruin within it, and the liberum veto let a single objection undo a whole parliament.
889._accuracy_note: A strong fit for how a tiny dissent can carry great harm, though historians treat the veto as one of several causes of the Commonwealth's fall.

890.event_title: The First Triumvirate of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus
890.event: Around 60 BCE Julius Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed an unofficial and at first secret political alliance, now called the First Triumvirate, each seeking his own ends. The partnership was renewed at Luca in 56 BCE, but the death of Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, in 54 BCE and of Crassus in 53 BCE removed its bonds, and Pompey drew closer to Caesar's opponents in the Senate. In January 49 BCE the Senate decreed a state of emergency against Caesar, and he crossed the Rubicon, beginning a civil war in which Pompey was defeated and killed.
890.explanation: The three men shared power without sharing purpose, and their uneasy partnership ended in war between two of them.
890.tie_back: The kural likens living with those who lack inner agreement to sharing a hut with a snake, which describes the alliance that ended with Caesar and Pompey at war.
890._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of an alliance without inner agreement; the kural's image is of daily dread, which the sources do not document for these men.
